# How This Document Works

This document describes **step by step how we proceed** and shows the corresponding code.
The code itself lives in **scripts**, one per module:

| Folder | Contents | Loaded … |
|---|---|---|
| `R/` | Functions and settings (`00_setup.R` … `70_validierung.R`) | automatically, via `source("R/laden.R")` |
| `skripte/` | Actions: import, translation setup, analyses, validation | manually only |

Script sections are marked with `## ---- name ----`. This document pulls them in via
`knitr::read_chunk()`: each code chunk below shows exactly the section of the same name. When a
script changes, this document is up to date the next time it is knitted. The code therefore
lives in **one place only**.
Long-running R processes keep the outlet configuration loaded from startup. If outlets are added
while one is already running, `Rscript skripte/b3_import_aufstockung.R` imports those sources with
separate progress markers and without loading a second GPU model.

There are two kinds of code chunks:

| Kind | Recognisable by | What happens when knitting? |
|---|---|---|
| **Function and configuration chunks** | no `eval = FALSE` | run: they define settings and functions |
| **Action chunks** (import, translation, analyses) | `eval = FALSE` | **not** run automatically |

You run action chunks **manually** in RStudio (cursor in the chunk, `Ctrl + Shift + Enter`;
RStudio ignores `eval = FALSE` here). This way, knitting the document can never accidentally
start a job that runs for hours or costs money.

The **nightly run** (Section 7) loads all functions via `source("R/laden.R")` and then works
through pending translations.

## The Workflow at a Glance

1. **Configuration:** countries, outlets, periods
2. **Database:** a single SQLite file holds all articles and translations, including their status
3. **Data collection:** read Nexis exports, add scraper output (e.g. the tagesschau pilot)
4. **Preprocessing:** assign periods, cut title/lead/half page, coarse filter, duplicates
5. **Local translation (NLLB):** all titles and leads, then the half page
6. **Translation cross-check (planned):** a second local model (HY-MT2, not installed yet) translates a sample, no cloud service involved
7. **Staged nightly run**
8. **Fine-grained relevance filter** in English
9. **Analysis corpus and DTM**
10. **Dictionaries and keywords in context**
11. **Structural topic model**
12. **Source attribution** (all countries)
13. **Validation:** relevance, sources, translation quality

> **Core methodological decision on translation:** The main analysis uses the local NLLB
> translation for **all** countries. Every country thus passes through the same translation
> engine, so cross-country differences are not artefacts of different translators.
> UK and Irish articles enter in their English original. A second, locally run translation model
> (planned: HY-MT2) translates a sample as a **cross-check**: if the English versions hardly differ,
> machine translation is not a problem. De Vries, Schoonvelde and Schumacher (2018, *Political
> Analysis*; page still to be verified) show that machine translation is adequate for
> bag-of-words methods.

```{r pakete}
```

## Folders and Secret Keys

All data live under `data/`. This folder is excluded from the repository via `.gitignore`,
because **the full-text corpus must not be published** (§ 60d UrhG, the German copyright
provision for text and data mining; outlets' terms of use).

Never write the **Media Cloud key** (optional, section “Scraping All Countries”) into the code. Put it in
the file `.Renviron` in the project folder (also listed in `.gitignore`):

```
MEDIACLOUD_API_KEY=dein-schluessel-hier
```

Then restart R. `Sys.getenv("MEDIACLOUD_API_KEY")` will read it.

```{r ordner}
```

## Parallel Computing

Your machine has several CPU cores, but R uses only one by default. The packages `future` and
`furrr` distribute work across several **workers**: independent R processes running in the
background (`multisession` mode, which also works on Windows).

**Where it pays off and where it does not:**

| Step | Parallel? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Preprocessing (cutting lead/half page) | yes | purely CPU-bound, many articles |
| Sentence-level source attribution analysis | yes | many sentences, independent of each other |
| quanteda (tokens, DTM, dictionaries) | yes | quanteda uses its own threads |
| STM: testing several K (`searchK`) | yes | each K is a separate model |
| Scraping **several outlets** | yes | one worker per outlet, pauses are kept |
| Scraping **within one outlet** | **no** | courtesy pauses, otherwise we risk being blocked |
| Translation (NLLB) | **no** | runs on the GPU, where batch size is what helps |

**Costs:** Each worker receives a **copy** of the data it needs. This costs start-up time and
memory, so for small tasks parallel execution is actually slower. The functions below
therefore switch to parallel mode only for larger amounts of data.

By default, `kerne` (cores) leaves **2 cores free** so the PC stays usable during long runs.
On a Ryzen 7 5800X3D (16 threads), that means 14 workers.

```{r parallel}
```

# Configuration

All research design decisions are kept here **in one place**. If you swap an outlet or shift
a period, for example, you only change this section.

## Countries

All countries in the sample are on the same level. There is no ranking by importance, and all
analyses, including the source analysis, cover all countries.

For an overview of the available data, we first collect **6 national outlets each in all 28 countries
(EU27 + UK)**. Which of them enter the analysis will be decided in light of the data
available; the justification for the selection is still outstanding.

```{r laender}
```

## Languages and Language Codes

Each language needs a code for **NLLB** (local model, format `xxx_Script`). Language is tied to the **outlet**, not the country, because Belgium, for example,
has outlets in Dutch and in French.

```{r sprachen}
```

## Outlets

Six national outlets per country: at least one public broadcaster, the rest private, spread across
the political spectrum where possible. Each sixth outlet is exploratory and remains unclassified
(`unklar`) until its orientation is documented. The columns:

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `traeger` (ownership) | `oeffentlich-rechtlich` (public broadcaster) or `privat` (private) |
| `ausrichtung` (orientation) | provisional placement from left … right; before the exposé, back it up with the Media Pluralism Monitor or the Reuters Digital News Report |
| `typ`, `paywall` | quality newspaper, tabloid, broadcaster, online; paywall yes/partial/no |
| `zugang` (access) | best route to the full texts: `nexis`, `wiso`, `paperboy` (ready-made parser) or `scraper` |
| `sammler` (collector) | how the article URLs are found: own archive scraper (`tagesschau`, `guardian`, `err`) or generic (`sitemap`) |

We compared the original 140 national outlets against the source lists of Nexis Uni and wiso on
07.10.2026. The 28 additions are assigned to the scraper for now; Nexis
and wiso coverage has not been rechecked for them. First run
`Rscript skripte/b2_alle_scrapen.R aufstockung-nur-urls 0` to collect Sitemaps and Media Cloud
URLs sequentially using source-specific caches. If Media Cloud is queried as a separate job, let it
finish, then merge its results into the existing URL lists with
`Rscript skripte/b2_alle_scrapen.R aufstockung-nur-mc 0` (without crawling Sitemaps again). Then
fetch full texts sequentially with
`Rscript skripte/b2_alle_scrapen.R aufstockung-nur-volltexte 0`. Articles of licensed outlets and
of outlets that do not allow automated retrieval are exported from Nexis Uni (see
`nexis/README.md`). Paywalls are not bypassed.

```{r medien}
```

## Periods and Control Sample

We do not collect continuously but in **six event periods** (F1–F6) around key events. On
import, each article receives its code in the variable `zeitraum` (period): F1–F6, or K for
control days. Together with `land` (country), this is the second central comparison variable:
differences between periods show how coverage changes with events; differences between
countries show how much coverage diverges at the same point in time. **Check the dates
against a chronology before submitting the exposé.**

In addition, there is a **control sample from routine periods**: constructed weeks. For each
constructed week, one random Monday, Tuesday … Sunday is drawn from the full study period,
but only from days **outside** the event periods. The sample thus reflects the weekly rhythm
of news coverage without being dominated by peak phases. The fixed `seed` makes the draw
reproducible.

```{r zeitraeume}
```

## Per-Outlet Glossary

NLLB mistranslates some names, either because they are also ordinary words in the source
language (Estonian “Saks” is a surname but also means “German”), or because they are proper
names that should not be translated (the ERR news programme “Aktuaalne kaamera” became
“Current Camera”). The glossary defines **per outlet** which terms are replaced by a
placeholder before translation and reinserted in a fixed form afterwards (see the NLLB
section).

- `muster` (pattern): regular expression in the **original** (cover inflected forms with `\\w*`)
- `englisch` (English): fixed form in the translation
- `medium = "*"`: applies to all outlets

The glossary grows with validation: whenever a name is repeatedly mistranslated in the
output, it is added here.

```{r glossar}
```

## Text and Translation Parameters

- **`lead_zeichen`** (lead characters): the “lead” is the first ~400 characters, trimmed to
  the end of a sentence. Not every source has its own lead field, so this keeps the
  definition consistent across sources.
- **`halbseite_zeichen`** (half-page characters): ~1,500 characters, roughly half an A4 page.
- **`validierung_n`**: number of articles that a second local model additionally translates (cross-check).

```{r parameter}
```

# Database

## Why a Database Instead of CSV Files?

The pipeline runs for weeks in many small steps. Each step needs to know **what has already
been done**. An SQLite database is a single file (`data/korpus.sqlite`), needs no server, and
can be read and written by several sessions in turn. If a run aborts, everything up to the
last saved batch is preserved.

Three tables:

| Table | Contents |
|---|---|
| `artikel` | one record per article: metadata, original text, lead, half page, filter status |
| `uebersetzung` | one row per translated field and engine (`titel`/`lead`/`halbseite` × `nllb`; the cross-check later uses `hymt2`) |
| `lauf_log` | log of every nightly run: when, what, how many characters |

```{r db-funktionen}
```

# Data Collection

## Common Format

Regardless of its origin, every article is converted into the same format and written to the
database through **one** function. This step also performs all preprocessing (Section 5).
`INSERT OR IGNORE` ensures that an article imported twice is stored only once. The ID is a
hash of outlet, date and title, so it stays stable across imports.

```{r funktion-import}
```

## Nexis Uni

For most newspapers, Nexis Uni is the access point. Procedure in the database:

1. Search per outlet and period, e.g. `Gaza OR Israel OR Palästin* OR Hamas OR Westjordanland`
   in the respective national language (document the search strings per language; they belong
   in the methods chapter!).
2. Export hits in batches as **.docx** (Nexis Uni limits the number per download).
3. Store the files under `data/raw/nexis/<Land>/<Medium>/`.

The package `LexisNexisTools` reads these exports and separates metadata (newspaper, date,
title) from the text. The newspaper name in Nexis often differs from ours, e.g.
“The Guardian (London)”. The table `nexis_namen` (Nexis names) maps these; after the first
import, add the names the script reports as “nicht in der Konfiguration” (“not in the
configuration”).

```{r funktion-nexis}
```

```{r nexis-import, eval = FALSE}
```

## Custom Scrapers

Each scraper returns a CSV with the columns `medium, datum, titel, text, url` and stores it
under `data/raw/scraper/` (the tagesschau pilot under `data/processed/`). Three are finished
and tested:

### tagesschau.de (`R/11_scraper_tagesschau.R`)

The **monthly archive** (`tagesschau.de/archiv?datum=JJJJ-MM-01&pageIndex=N`) lists all items
of a month, about 500 entries across 4–5 pages. The search interface reaches back only about
four weeks and is therefore unsuitable. Full texts are in `p.textabsatz` and
`h2.meldung__subhead`. We exclude live blogs (those before October 2024 have been depublished
anyway). Details: `01_pilot_tagesschau.Rmd`.

```{r tagesschau-archiv}
```

```{r tagesschau-volltext}
```

### The Guardian (`R/12_scraper_guardian.R`)

Each tag has a **daily archive**
(`theguardian.com/world/israel-hamas-war/2023/oct/10/all`). We collect the links for the tags
war, Gaza and West Bank and keep only articles and comment pieces. Live blogs, videos, audio
and galleries are dropped. `medium_scrapen()` (below) fetches the full texts. The text is in
`div.article-body-commercial-selector`, the date in the meta tag `article:published_time`. In
the research design, the Guardian comes via Nexis; the scraper serves as a supplement and
cross-check.

```{r guardian-funktionen}
```

### ERR, Estonia (`R/13_scraper_err.R`)

err.ee loads its lists through a **JSON interface**. We combine the **daily list of all news
items** (`/api/category/latest/109`, coarse filter on title and lead) with the **search**
(`/api/search/getContents/`, several Estonian word forms). In testing, the daily list added
only 3 articles beyond the search. The text is in `article.prime div.text p`.

```{r err-funktionen}
```

### Importing the Results

```{r scraper-import, eval = FALSE}
```

## Scraping Several Outlets in Parallel

For freely accessible outlets without Nexis access. `medium_scrapen()` (scrape outlet) fetches
the articles of **one** outlet sequentially, with pauses and a cache. `mehrere_medien_scrapen()`
(scrape several outlets) starts a separate worker for each outlet. ERR, LSM and LRT, for
example, thus run simultaneously, while each site is still queried only every `pause` seconds.

Each outlet needs a URL list and the CSS selectors for title, date and text. You have to
identify these for each site in the browser (right-click → “Inspect”) and test them on a few
articles. The result is saved as a CSV in `data/raw/scraper/` and imported into the database
with the “scraper-import” chunk.

```{r funktion-scraper}
```

```{r scraper-parallel-beispiel, eval = FALSE}
```

In an early test run with three countries, the Guardian and ERR ran in
parallel this way, with these selectors:

| Outlet | `selektor_text` | `selektor_titel` | Date |
|---|---|---|---|
| The Guardian | `div.article-body-commercial-selector > p, … > h2` | `h1` | `meta[property='article:published_time']`, attribute `content` |
| ERR | `article.prime div.text p` | `article.prime h1` | from the search interface |

## Scraping All Countries

For 168 national outlets plus regional and other sources you cannot look for archives and CSS selectors by hand. The generic scraper
(`R/14_url_sammler.R`, `R/15_volltext.R`, `R/16_alle_medien.R`) does this automatically, in
three steps per outlet.

**1. Find article URLs.** Three routes, whose results are combined:

- **Own archive scrapers** for tagesschau, the Guardian and ERR (see above).
- **Sitemaps:** Almost every news site publishes a list of all its article URLs for search
  engines, usually split by month or day. Where it lives is stated in the `robots.txt`. We read
  only the sub-sitemaps whose name or modification date falls within our period.
- **Media Cloud** (optional): a freely usable news archive with full-text search. With a free
  account on search.mediacloud.org and the key in `.Renviron` (`MEDIACLOUD_API_KEY=…`), the
  scraper additionally searches there for articles on the conflict. This helps with sites whose
  URLs contain no keywords (e.g. only an article number).
  Because Media Cloud only allows about 10 requests per minute per account, we query it **once
  up front** for all outlets together, and only for the study periods F1–F6 (month by month)
  and the control days (`mc_fenster()`, `mc_alle_urls()`) and then assign the hits to the outlets by domain. Every finished month is
  saved (`data/raw/urls/_mediacloud/`), so an interrupted run resumes there.

The other URLs are also kept only if their date falls within a study period or on a control
day (or is unknown).

**2. Coarse filtering.** The sitemaps return all articles, including sport and weather. We
fetch only those whose URL (or sitemap title) points to the conflict (`url_relevanz_regex`,
multilingual, including transliterated forms such as the Greek “israil”). This is generous:
whatever slips through here is caught by the coarse filter on the text later. What the URL does
not reveal, we find only via Media Cloud or the archive scrapers.

**3. Fetch and parse full texts.** One outlet at a time with a pause, all outlets in parallel.
Each page is saved once (`data/raw/html/<Medium>/`); an interrupted run resumes there on the
next start. When parsing, we try three routes and take the longest usable text: the matching
**paperboy** parser (if one exists for the domain), **JSON-LD** (a machine-readable article
description that many sites embed for search engines) and general rules (`article p`,
`main p`).

**Rules the scraper follows:**

- If the `robots.txt` blocks all crawlers, we skip the outlet; blocked paths are not fetched.
  A specified `Crawl-delay` is honoured.
- Paywalls are not circumvented. If a text is only a teaser, `paywall_hinweis` (paywall note)
  flags it; these outlets come via Nexis or wiso.
- The user agent states purpose and contact (`kontakt` in `R/10_scraper_allgemein.R`).
- Nexis and wiso are not queried automatically (licence terms). There we export by hand, in
  batches.

```{r url-grundlagen}
```

```{r robots}
```

```{r sitemaps}
```

```{r url-relevanz}
```

```{r mediacloud}
```

```{r spezial-sammler}
```

```{r volltext-holen}
```

```{r volltext-parsen}
```

```{r medium-sammeln}
```


# Preprocessing

## Cleaning Text, Cutting Lead and Half Page

`kuerzen_auf_satz()` (trim to sentence) cuts a text to at most `n` characters **but always ends
on a complete sentence**. From 10,000 texts upwards, this runs in parallel (see “Parallel Computing”). A truncated half-sentence would degrade the translation.
If there is no sentence end within the range (e.g. an extremely long sentence), the text is
cut at the last space.

```{r funktion-vorverarbeitung}
```

## Coarse Filter in the Original Language

The coarse filter is **deliberately generous**: it only removes obviously irrelevant material
before computing time goes into translation. The actual relevance check happens later in
English (Section 8). The word stems cover all 20 languages; have native speakers review them
when possible.

```{r grobfilter}
```

## Duplicates: Republished Wire Stories

Many outlets run the same AFP, Reuters or dpa story almost verbatim. We need to translate it
only **once**. We flag an article as a duplicate if its lead (normalised: lower case, no
punctuation, first 300 characters) already occurs in the same language. The duplicate points
to the oldest article via `dublette_von` (duplicate of) and later inherits its translation.

For the **analysis**, duplicates stay in the corpus: an outlet's decision to run a wire story
is part of its coverage. This simple matching finds only near-identical stories; lightly
rewritten wire copy slips through. This is uncritical for costs.

```{r funktion-dubletten}
```

```{r dubletten-ausfuehren, eval = FALSE}
```

# Local Translation with NLLB

## What Is NLLB, and Why Run It Locally?

**NLLB-200** (“No Language Left Behind”) is a freely available translation model from Meta
that covers all our languages. It runs on your own PC, **so it costs nothing** but electricity
and time. On the GPU it is many times faster than on the CPU. Its licence (CC-BY-NC) permits
non-commercial research, which covers a master's thesis.

R talks to the model through **`reticulate`**, the bridge to Python.

**AMD graphics card (RX 9070 XT) on Windows:** PyTorch runs here via **ROCm**, AMD's counterpart
to CUDA. AMD provides dedicated Python packages for this (ROCm 7.2.1 for Windows). Requirements
according to AMD's guide: **Python 3.12** and **AMD Adrenalin driver 26.2.2 or newer**. If
PyTorch still does not detect the card, everything continues on the CPU, just more slowly.

One-time setup (downloads about 2 GB in total, plus 2.5 GB for the model on first load).
We use **`uv`**, a fast Python package manager that reticulate uses anyway. It ships its own
Python 3.12 (no admin rights, nothing system-wide) and creates the environment where
reticulate finds it under the name `masterarbeit`.

```{r nllb-einrichten, eval = FALSE}
```

## Translating Sentence by Sentence

NLLB is trained on **single sentences**. Given several sentences at once, it drops or merges
sentences and even invents content. In an early three-country test run, translations of ~600-character
chunks were on average 30% shorter than the original. One translation turned “Aktuaalne
kaamera” (the ERR news programme) into the “New York Times”. We therefore translate **sentence
by sentence** (paragraphs and subheadings count as sentence boundaries) and reassemble the
sentences afterwards. With `num_beams = 4`, the model considers several candidate translations
instead of only the first.

## Protecting Names and Sources

For the source analysis, it is crucial that names and source attributions survive translation.
In the example, “vahendas Reuters Gaza allikaid” (“Reuters reported, citing sources in Gaza”)
became just “sources in Gaza said”: Reuters was gone, and the expert “Rainer Saks” became
“Germany”.

We therefore request the **four best translations** for each sentence and keep the one that
contains the most **protected terms**. In case of a tie, the variant the model itself scores
highest wins. Protected terms are:

- **Agencies and outlets** from a fixed list (Reuters, AFP, dpa, BBC, IDF …), even when they are
  inflected in the original (Estonian “Reutersi” → “Reuters” is required)
- **Names**: two consecutive capitalised words such as “Rainer Saks” or
  “Annalena Baerbock”. In German, this also catches word pairs such as “Bundeskanzler Olaf”
  (“Chancellor Olaf”). This does no harm: a term that no variant contains does not affect the
  selection.

The selection can only replace a poor translation with another one **generated by the model
itself**. It therefore adds nothing that the model did not produce.

In addition, the **per-outlet glossary** applies (see the Configuration section): glossary terms
are replaced before translation by placeholders (`ZZ01`, `ZZ02` …), which NLLB passes through
unchanged, and are then replaced by the fixed English form. The **source language** is always
determined by the outlet, not by the model. Language detection (`cld2`) only checks on import
whether the text is actually in that language. If it is not, the article is not translated but
flagged for review via `sprache_pruefen()` (check language).

## Model Choice: 600M or 1.3B?

NLLB comes in several sizes. Tested on 4 October 2026 on 25 relevant articles each from
tagesschau and ERR (half page, sentence by sentence, RX 9070 XT):

| Variant | Time for 50 texts | Length EN/original (median) | Agencies preserved | Names preserved |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 600M | 15 s | 0.96 | 14/14 | 97.4% |
| 600M + protection | 14 s | 0.96 | 14/14 | 98.7% |
| 1.3B | 24 s | 0.96 | 14/14 | 100% |
| 1.3B + protection | 23 s | 0.96 | 14/14 | 100% |

(“Names preserved”: name pairs such as “Alar Karis” that appear verbatim in at least one
variant. Measured on 78 names.)

Example: 600M turned “president Alar Karis” into “President Alaris”, with protection into
“President Al-Alar Karis”, and 1.3B correctly into “President Alar Karis”. **Decision: 1.3B with
protection.** It is about 60% slower but more reliable on names, which the source analysis
depends on. Extrapolated to 20,000 half pages, this takes just under 3 hours, i.e. one night.

```{r funktion-nllb}
```

---

# Staged Nightly Run

## Order of Work

The nightly run works through a **priority list**. Each step specifies which field is
translated by which engine for which articles. Only when a step is fully completed does the
run move on to the next.

| # | Field | Engine | Articles | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Title | NLLB | all passing the coarse filter | relevance filter |
| 2 | Lead | NLLB | all passing the coarse filter | relevance filter, then: compute relevance |
| 3 | Half page | NLLB | all relevant | **main analysis** |

English-language articles (UK, Ireland) are never translated; the original is used.

```{r schritte}
```

## Finding Pending Jobs and Processing a Batch

`offene_auftraege()` (pending jobs) queries the database: which articles still need a
translation for this step? Excluded are duplicates (they inherit the translation),
English-language articles and anything that failed the coarse filter.

`paket_uebersetzen()` (translate batch) fetches a batch, translates it **per language** and
saves immediately. The return value tells the nightly run how to proceed: the number of
translated texts, `0` = step complete.

```{r funktion-paket}
```

## The Nightly Run

`naechtlicher_lauf()` (nightly run) works through the steps in order until the time is up. It
deliberately runs **without** CPU parallelisation: the bottleneck is the GPU, and
multiple workers would only occupy the GPU several times over. Every error
is written to the log instead of aborting the run. The NLLB model is loaded only
when a local step actually has work to do.

```{r funktion-nachtlauf}
```

## Starting Automatically Every Night (Windows)

The file `run_nightly.R` in the repository loads all functions via `source("R/laden.R")` and
calls `naechtlicher_lauf()`. The
Windows Task Scheduler starts it every night at 1 a.m. Run once:

```{r aufgabe-anlegen, eval = FALSE}
```

You can check progress at any time like this:

```{r stand, eval = FALSE}
```

# Fine-Grained Relevance Filter in English

After steps 1 and 2, titles and leads of all articles are available in English. We now check
more closely whether an article is **actually about the Israel–Palestine conflict** rather than,
say, the war with Iran or in Lebanon, in which Israel also features.

The rule:

- **Palestine terms** (Gaza, West Bank, Palestin*, Hamas, Rafah, Jenin, settler, UNRWA …)
  must occur at least once,
- and at least as often as **regional terms** (Iran, Hezbollah, Lebanon, Houthi …).
- If no Palestine term occurs but “Israel” does, the article also counts
  (e.g. Israeli domestic politics relating to the war), provided **no** regional term occurs.
  (Previously, “Israel” had to occur twice. In an early three-country test run, this excluded
  relevant Guardian articles because titles and leads are short.)

You validate this on a sample (Section 13).

```{r funktion-relevanz}
```

## Drawing the Sample for the Translation Cross-Check

Once relevance is determined, we draw, once, the articles whose half page is **additionally**
translated by a second local translation model (planned: HY-MT2). The sample is stratified by language so
that every language is represented. No text leaves the computer.

```{r validierung-ziehen, eval = FALSE}
```

# Analysis Corpus and DTM

## Building the Corpus from the Database

For each article we need the English text. The rules:

- **English originals** (UK, IE): original.
- **All others:** NLLB translation.
- **Duplicates:** translation of the original article.

The analysis uses `titel_en + halbseite_en`. The half page begins with the lead; appending
the lead again would double its weight.

```{r funktion-korpus}
```

```{r korpus-bauen, eval = FALSE}
```

## Tokens and DTM

As in the pilot, now in English:

1. Tokenise, remove punctuation, numbers and URLs, convert to lower case
2. Merge **multi-word expressions** (`west_bank`, `israeli_army` …), otherwise they fall apart
3. Remove English stop words and news-language filler words
4. Build the DTM; for topic models, remove rare words (in < 10 articles)

We keep the **tokens** (before the DTM): the dictionaries work on them because there they can
also match multi-word expressions such as “ethnic cleansing”.

```{r dtm, eval = FALSE}
```

---

# Dictionaries and KWIC

## Removing Boilerplate

Some parsers also pick up teasers for other articles, menus, image credits or newsletter
notices. The Slovak Pravda, for instance, carried the teaser "Abbas: Palestinians have a right
to defend themselves …" in about 690 articles. Sentences that appear **verbatim in at least 15
articles of the same outlet** are therefore removed before all dictionary analyses. This also
covers recurring agency background paragraphs ("In response to the Hamas assault …"): the frames
should measure what the outlet itself chooses, not stock text (decision of 08.10.2026, see
`ENTSCHEIDUNGEN.md`).

```{r textbausteine, eval = FALSE}
```

## English Discourse Dictionary

The categories follow the research questions. **Important:** a match only means that a term
**appears in the article**, not that the outlet endorses it. KWIC and the source analysis
clarify what lies behind it.

```{r woerterbuch, eval = FALSE}
```

## Self-defence in the Israeli Context

The frame “Self-defence” measures whether self-defence is invoked or discussed in the Israeli context. A sentence
counts if it contains the term and refers neither to the Palestinians’ right to defend themselves nor to
another conflict (e.g. Ukraine), and does not deny self-defence (“This is not self-defence”). The rules are checked on samples and
validated in section 13.3.

```{r selbstverteidigung, eval = FALSE}
```


## KWIC: Who Says “Genocide”?

```{r kwic, eval = FALSE}
```

---

# Structural Topic Model

## Idea

A topic model identifies themes that co-occur in articles without our specifying them in
advance. The **structural** topic model (Roberts et al., *American Journal of Political
Science* 2014; page still to be verified) additionally allows the **prevalence of a topic** to
depend on covariates, in our case country and period. This is exactly what the comparison
requires: which country writes more about the “humanitarian situation” in which period, and
which more about “security and terrorism”?

## Choosing the Number of Topics

There is no “correct” K. `searchK()` compares metrics (semantic coherence, exclusivity,
held-out likelihood) across several values of K. In the end, you decide based on
**interpretability** and document the choice.

**Parallel:** each K is a separate model, so we fit each K in its own worker. The built-in
`cores` argument of `searchK()` does not work on Windows, hence `furrr`. **Watch the memory:**
each worker holds a copy of the DTM. With 32 GB RAM, 5 workers (one per K) is a good value. If
memory gets tight, reduce `workers`.

```{r stm-k, eval = FALSE}
```

```{r stm-modell, eval = FALSE}
```

# Source Attribution

As in the pilot, now in English and for all countries. For each sentence we check:

1. Does it contain an **attribution pattern** (“according to”, “said”, “claimed” …)?
2. Which **actor** is named?
3. Is there a **verification caveat** (“could not be independently verified”)?

Two limitations belong in the thesis: translation can smooth over attributions
(e.g. “behauptete” (“claimed”) → “said”), which is why we validate against original sentences
(Section 13); and the sentence level does not capture attributions that span several sentences.

```{r quellen-muster}
```

```{r quellen-analyse, eval = FALSE}
```

## German Patterns for the Original (Validation)

For German-language outlets, the patterns developed in the pilot are also available in German.
They serve to **validate** the English patterns against the original sentence. They also
contain the context rule for the **Ministry of Health**, which exists both in Israel and in
Gaza. The assignment is based on the sentence itself, the last unambiguous mention in the
article, and otherwise the three preceding sentences. In the pilot, this assigned all 23
mentions correctly.

```{r quellen-muster-de}
```

```{r funktion-saetze-markieren-de}
```

# Validation

Without validation, automated measurements cannot be used in the thesis. Three checks:

## 13.1 Relevance Filter

Draw 200 articles (half classified as relevant, half as not relevant), code them by hand and
compute precision and recall.

```{r val-relevanz-export, eval = FALSE}
```

```{r funktion-guete}
```

```{r val-relevanz-auswerten, eval = FALSE}
```

## 13.2 Source Attribution, with a Second Coder

Draw 300 sentences and output them **in the original and in English**. You and a second person
code them independently. Krippendorff's alpha shows whether you agree (≥ 0.8 is considered
good); precision/recall then measures how well the patterns perform.

```{r val-quellen, eval = FALSE}
```

## 13.3 Frames on Original Sentences

For each dictionary category, 40 matching sentences (for self-defence, by the sentence rules),
shuffled and without the machine category. Coders decide whether the frame applies. The result is precision per frame; below about 0.8 the
dictionary is refined.

```{r val-frames, eval = FALSE}
```

## 13.4 Translation Quality: NLLB vs. a Second Local Model

For the sample (`validierung = 1`), the half page is available in **both** translations (`nllb` and
`hymt2`; the second model is not installed yet). We test whether the dictionary measurement yields the same
results with both engines. If it does, the translation is sufficient for our purposes, which is the argument
for basing the main analysis on NLLB. There is no judge model and nothing is written back.

```{r val-uebersetzung, eval = FALSE}
```
